prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- U.S. health officials said Wednesday they have found a contaminant in a blood-thinning drug produced by Baxter Healthcare Corp. that has been linked to more than a dozen deaths in the United States. The drug can keep potentially life-threatening blood clots from forming in the veins, arteries, and lungs. In early February, the Food and Drug Administration launched an investigation and then a recall of some forms of the product. The scrutiny began after a spike in reports of health problems associated with heparin, a drug made by Baxter from pig intestines at plants in China and Wisconsin. Though the cause of the problems has not been determined, FDA investigators found "a heparin-like compound -- that is not heparin -- present in some of the active pharmaceutical ingredients" in both facilities, said Dr. Janet Woodcock, acting director of the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. The contaminant, which made up 5 percent to 20 percent of each sample tested, "reacts like heparin in some of the conventional tests used for heparin," which explains why it was not picked up, she told reporters in a conference call. No causal link between the contaminant and the adverse events has been established yet, Woodcock said. She added that it was not clear whether the contaminant was added accidentally, as part of the processing or deliberately. It also was not clear whether the contaminant was introduced in the company's plant in Wisconsin or the one in China, Woodcock said. Though she said the exact structure of the contaminant has not been identified, "it is similar to heparin glycans." Glycans are polysaccharides, a complex class of carbohydrate. She added it was unclear whether other heparin products used outside the United States might also contain the product. Later this week, the agency will release recommendations on how manufacturers and regulators can screen for the contaminant, she said. Last year, pet food made in China was found to be tainted with an ingredient that replaced more expensive protein and that initial tests did not identify as a contaminant. Asked if the heparin contamination could be a similar case, Woodcock said, "It's possible." Doctors have used the blood-thinner for 60 years with "no history of any problems whatsoever," said the FDA commissioner, Dr. Andrew C. von Eschenbach. Its intravenous use can keep potentially life-threatening blood clots from forming in the veins, arteries and lungs. Von Eschenbach said it would be "disingenuous" to expect the agency would be able to inspect "every institution in every case." Over the last fiscal year, the agency reported having inspected more than 1,000 foreign plants, a record. Since the agency issued its report that 19 deaths had been linked to the drug since January 1, 2007, it has received word of another 27 deaths, "but many of those do not fit our definition of this type of event," Woodcock said. In all, the FDA has received 785 heparin-linked reports of adverse events -- including difficulty breathing, nausea, vomiting, excessive sweating and plummeting blood pressure that can lead to life-threatening shock. "They're continuing to come in fairly rapidly because there has been a lot of reporting of this," she said. In a written statement, Baxter said its tests have suggested "that the root cause may be associated with the crude heparin, sourced from China, or from the subsequent processing of that product before it reaches Baxter." Meanwhile, Scientific Protein Laboratories LLC, which supplies the company with the active pharmaceutical ingredients, issued a statement saying it is working with the FDA, Baxter and outside experts to identify the cause of the adverse events. "Thus far, no conclusions have been reached about the root cause," it said. "It is premature to conclude that the heparin active pharmaceutical ingredient sourced from China and provided by SPL to Baxter is responsible for these adverse events." It said that its voluntary recall of suspect product was being made as a precaution.  E-mail to a friend .

**(CNN) —** U.S. health officials said Wednesday that they had identified a contaminant in a blood-thinning drug produced by Baxter Healthcare Corp. that has been linked to more than a dozen deaths in the United States.

The drug, heparin, can prevent potentially life-threatening blood clots from forming in the veins, arteries, and lungs. In early February, the Food and Drug Administration launched an investigation and subsequently recalled some forms of the product.

The scrutiny began following a surge in reports of health problems associated with heparin, which Baxter manufactures from pig intestines at plants in China and Wisconsin.

Although the cause of the problems has not been determined, FDA investigators found “a heparin-like compound—that is not heparin—present in some of the active pharmaceutical ingredients” at both facilities, according to Dr. Janet Woodcock, acting director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research.

The contaminant, which accounted for 5 percent to 20 percent of each sample tested, “reacts like heparin in some of the conventional tests used for heparin,” explaining why it had not previously been detected, Woodcock told reporters during a conference call.

No causal link between the contaminant and the adverse events has yet been established, Woodcock said. She added that it remained unclear whether the contaminant had been introduced accidentally, as part of the manufacturing process, or deliberately. It was also uncertain whether the contaminant originated at the company’s Wisconsin plant or its facility in China.

Although the contaminant’s precise structure has not been identified, Woodcock said that “it is similar to heparin glycans.” Glycans are polysaccharides, a complex class of carbohydrates.

She added that it was unclear whether other heparin products used outside the United States might also contain the contaminant. Later this week, the agency will issue recommendations on how manufacturers and regulators can screen for it, she said.

Last year, pet food manufactured in China was found to have been tainted with an ingredient that substituted for more expensive protein and was not identified as a contaminant in initial testing. Asked whether the heparin contamination could be a similar case, Woodcock replied, “It’s possible.”

Doctors have used the blood thinner for 60 years with “no history of any problems whatsoever,” said FDA Commissioner Dr. Andrew C. von Eschenbach. When administered intravenously, the drug can prevent potentially life-threatening blood clots from forming in the veins, arteries, and lungs.

Von Eschenbach said it would be “disingenuous” to expect the agency to inspect “every institution in every case.” During the last fiscal year, the agency reported inspecting more than 1,000 foreign plants—a record.

Since the agency reported that 19 deaths had been linked to the drug since January 1, 2007, it has received reports of an additional 27 deaths, “but many of those do not fit our definition of this type of event,” Woodcock said.

In total, the FDA has received 785 reports of adverse events linked to heparin, including difficulty breathing, nausea, vomiting, excessive sweating, and a sharp drop in blood pressure that can lead to life-threatening shock.

“They’re continuing to come in fairly rapidly because there has been a lot of reporting of this,” she said.

In a written statement, Baxter said its testing suggested “that the root cause may be associated with the crude heparin, sourced from China, or from the subsequent processing of that product before it reaches Baxter.”

Meanwhile, Scientific Protein Laboratories LLC, which supplies Baxter with the active pharmaceutical ingredients, said in a statement that it was working with the FDA, Baxter, and outside experts to identify the cause of the adverse events.

“Thus far, no conclusions have been reached about the root cause,” the company said. “It is premature to conclude that the heparin active pharmaceutical ingredient sourced from China and provided by SPL to Baxter is responsible for these adverse events.”

The company said its voluntary recall of the suspect product was being undertaken as a precaution.

(CNN) — Federal health authorities announced Wednesday that they had detected a foreign substance in a Baxter Healthcare Corp. anticoagulant associated with more than a dozen U.S. deaths.

The medication, heparin, is administered intravenously to prevent potentially fatal clots in the lungs, arteries and veins. After reports of medical complications involving the drug rose sharply, the Food and Drug Administration began investigating in early February and subsequently recalled certain versions of the product. Baxter manufactures heparin from pig intestines at facilities in China and Wisconsin.

Investigators have not determined what caused the reported reactions. However, testing at both plants revealed what Dr. Janet Woodcock, acting director of the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, described as a substance resembling heparin but not actually being heparin. The unidentified material accounted for 5% to 20% of the samples examined.

During a conference call with journalists, Woodcock explained that the substance behaves like heparin in some standard screening procedures, allowing it to escape detection. She said its precise chemical structure remained unknown, although it appeared similar to heparin glycans. Glycans are polysaccharides, a complex type of carbohydrate.

The FDA had not established that the contaminant caused the adverse reactions. Officials also could not say whether it entered the product accidentally during manufacturing or was added intentionally, nor whether it originated at the Wisconsin facility or the Chinese plant. Woodcock said it was also unknown whether heparin products marketed outside the United States might contain the same material.

The agency planned to issue guidance later that week explaining how regulators and manufacturers could test for the substance.

The discovery drew comparisons with a previous contamination case. In the prior year, Chinese-made pet food had been found to contain an ingredient substituted for more costly protein; initial testing failed to recognize it as a contaminant. When asked whether the heparin case might involve a similar situation, Woodcock replied that it was possible.

FDA Commissioner Dr. Andrew C. von Eschenbach noted that physicians had relied on the anticoagulant for six decades without any record of problems. He also said it would be unrealistic—or, in his words, “disingenuous”—to suggest that the FDA could inspect every facility in every instance. During the previous fiscal year, the agency had examined more than 1,000 overseas plants, the highest number in its history.

The FDA had earlier reported 19 deaths associated with heparin since January 1, 2007. It later learned of 27 additional fatalities, although Woodcock said many did not meet the agency’s criteria for the particular type of incident under investigation.

Altogether, the agency had received 785 reports of adverse events connected with heparin. Symptoms included breathing difficulties, nausea, vomiting, heavy sweating and a steep decline in blood pressure that could result in life-threatening shock. Woodcock said reports were still arriving relatively quickly because the issue had generated extensive reporting.

In a written response, Baxter said its testing indicated that the underlying problem might involve crude heparin obtained from China or processing carried out before the material arrived at Baxter.

Scientific Protein Laboratories LLC, Baxter’s supplier of the active pharmaceutical ingredients, said it was collaborating with the FDA, Baxter and independent specialists to determine what caused the reactions. The company emphasized that no definitive explanation had yet been found and said it was too early to conclude that the China-sourced active ingredient it provided to Baxter was responsible. Scientific Protein Laboratories added that it had voluntarily recalled the questionable product as a precaution.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report about U.S. health officials discovering a contaminant in Baxter Healthcare’s blood thinner heparin after reports of adverse reactions and deaths.
counterfactuals.output:
### Contaminant found in Baxter blood thinner amid reports of severe reactions

**WASHINGTON (CNN-style report)** — U.S. health officials say they have identified a contaminant in supplies of heparin, a widely used blood thinner, following hundreds of reports of allergic-type reactions and several deaths among patients who received the drug.

The Food and Drug Administration said testing of heparin produced by Baxter Healthcare found an altered substance known as **oversulfated chondroitin sulfate**. The contaminant closely resembles heparin chemically, making it difficult to detect through standard quality-control tests.

Officials said patients reported symptoms including dangerously low blood pressure, breathing problems, nausea and swelling. The FDA investigated deaths reported in people who had recently received heparin, although officials cautioned that not every death had been conclusively linked to the contaminant.

Baxter recalled affected heparin products and suspended production of certain injectable forms. The company’s active pharmaceutical ingredient had been supplied through a facility in China, prompting U.S. regulators to inspect the manufacturing operation and examine the broader international supply chain.

Heparin is commonly administered during dialysis, heart surgery and other medical procedures to prevent blood clots. Because it is considered an essential medication, health officials worked with other manufacturers to prevent shortages while contaminated products were removed.

The discovery raised concerns about oversight of foreign drug suppliers and the ability of regulators and manufacturers to detect substances deliberately or accidentally introduced into complex pharmaceutical ingredients. Investigators continued working to determine how and why the contaminant entered the heparin supply.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the FDA investigation into contaminated heparin sourced from plants in China and Wisconsin, including comments from Janet Woodcock, Andrew von Eschenbach, Baxter, and Scientific Protein Laboratories.
counterfactuals.output:
In 2008, the FDA investigated severe allergic-like reactions, hypotension, and deaths reported after patients received injectable heparin marketed by Baxter International. The active ingredient had been supplied by Scientific Protein Laboratories (SPL), which processed heparin at facilities in Changzhou, China, and Waunakee, Wisconsin. The raw material ultimately came from pig intestines collected through a complicated Chinese supply chain.

FDA scientists identified the contaminant as **oversulfated chondroitin sulfate (OSCS)**, a chemically modified, inexpensive substance that closely resembled heparin and could evade the standard quality tests then in use. OSCS was later shown to trigger biological pathways capable of producing the reactions seen in patients. Contaminated heparin or ingredients were found in multiple countries, although the FDA cautioned that not every reported death could be definitively attributed to the contaminant.

Key positions included:

- **Janet Woodcock**, then head of the FDA’s drug center, said the evidence indicated that the contamination entered the supply chain in China and appeared unlikely to be accidental. Because OSCS had been chemically altered to mimic heparin, officials considered economically motivated adulteration a strong possibility. She emphasized, however, that investigators had not determined precisely who introduced it or at what point.
- **FDA Commissioner Andrew von Eschenbach** said the episode exposed the difficulty of policing an increasingly global pharmaceutical supply chain. He defended the agency’s response while acknowledging weaknesses in overseas inspections and the need for a stronger permanent FDA presence abroad. The FDA had not inspected the Changzhou plant before it began supplying the U.S. market, in part because of an agency database error.
- **Baxter** recalled its heparin products, suspended production, and said it was cooperating with regulators. The company stated that the problem was in the active ingredient supplied to it rather than in Baxter’s final manufacturing process.
- **Scientific Protein Laboratories** also cooperated and tested material from both its Chinese and Wisconsin operations. SPL said the available evidence suggested the adulterant had entered the supply chain before the material reached its processing plants—likely through upstream Chinese crude-heparin suppliers—and cautioned against treating its Changzhou facility itself as the proven point of contamination.

The investigation ultimately prompted tighter heparin testing standards, broader inspections and recalls, and increased scrutiny of foreign drug-ingredient supply chains.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed breaking-news article explaining the 2008 Baxter heparin recall, the unidentified heparin-like contaminant, and the hundreds of adverse-event reports received by the FDA.
counterfactuals.output:
# Baxter Expands Heparin Recall as FDA Investigates Mysterious Contaminant, Hundreds of Adverse-Event Reports

**WASHINGTON, February 2008** — Baxter Healthcare is recalling nearly all remaining lots of its multidose injectable heparin after federal regulators detected an unidentified, heparin-like contaminant in the blood thinner and received hundreds of reports of allergic-type reactions, severe drops in blood pressure and other medical problems among patients.

The expanded recall, announced February 28, follows Baxter’s January withdrawal of nine lots of heparin sodium injection. It covers the company’s multidose vials as well as heparin flush products used to keep intravenous lines and catheters open. Certain premixed heparin solutions supplied in large-volume bags are not included, and regulators are warning hospitals not to abandon medically necessary treatment without suitable alternatives.

Heparin is one of the most widely used anticoagulants in hospitals. It is administered during kidney dialysis, cardiac surgery and other procedures to prevent potentially fatal blood clots. That central role has made the recall especially disruptive: Baxter had supplied a substantial share of the U.S. market, and health officials must balance the risk of suspect products against the danger of a shortage.

## Reports include hypotension, breathing difficulty and deaths

The Food and Drug Administration says it has received hundreds of adverse-event reports involving heparin products, including Baxter’s, since late 2007. Reports have described sudden low blood pressure, shortness of breath, nausea, vomiting, sweating, swelling and other symptoms resembling severe allergic or anaphylactoid reactions.

Some events occurred within minutes of an intravenous bolus or during dialysis. Deaths have also been reported in patients who received heparin, although the FDA stresses that a report does not by itself prove the drug caused an injury or death.

The agency’s adverse-event database is a warning system rather than a confirmed count of victims. Reports may be duplicated, incomplete or influenced by publicity; they often involve seriously ill patients taking multiple medications. Regulators therefore review medical records, lot numbers, timing and other evidence before deciding whether heparin contributed to an event.

Even with those limitations, the increase was striking enough to trigger inspections, laboratory testing and the broader recall.

## Standard quality tests failed to reveal the problem

FDA investigators say conventional tests initially indicated that the active pharmaceutical ingredient met the official standards for heparin. More sophisticated analyses, however, detected an additional substance that behaved chemically much like the drug itself.

Officials described the material at this stage as an unidentified “heparin-like” contaminant. It accounted for a significant portion of some tested samples and was difficult to distinguish from genuine heparin using the compendial methods then required.

That finding has raised urgent questions about whether the material was introduced accidentally during manufacturing, arose from inadequate purification or was deliberately added to imitate heparin and increase apparent potency. Regulators have not announced a definitive explanation and are cautioning against premature conclusions.

The suspect active ingredient was linked to a supply chain extending to China, where crude heparin is commonly extracted from pig intestines and then purified. Baxter’s finished products were made using active ingredient supplied through Scientific Protein Laboratories, which obtained material from a Chinese facility.

FDA officials and inspectors are examining records, equipment, raw-material controls and other companies that may have received related ingredients. The inquiry also focuses on the complicated network of workshops and consolidators involved in collecting porcine intestinal material.

## Recall is a precaution, not proof every vial is dangerous

Baxter says it is recalling the affected products because of the safety signals and contaminant findings, while cooperating with federal investigators. The company has advised customers to locate recalled lots, stop using them where alternatives are available and follow formal return instructions.

Neither Baxter nor the FDA has said that every recalled vial is contaminated. A nationwide recall can encompass large numbers of units because products from suspect lots or supply streams cannot be cleared individually with confidence.

Clinicians are being urged to check lot numbers, monitor patients closely and report suspected reactions through the FDA’s MedWatch program. Patients should not discontinue prescribed anticoagulation on their own, because untreated clotting can cause stroke, pulmonary embolism, heart attack or death.

## Later laboratory work identifies the substance

**Update:** In March 2008, after the contaminant was initially reported as unidentified, the FDA and collaborating laboratories identified it as **oversulfated chondroitin sulfate**, or OSCS.

OSCS is a chemically modified polysaccharide that can resemble heparin in common analytical and biological assays but is not an approved component of the drug. Subsequent research indicated that it could activate biological pathways associated with the abrupt hypotension and allergic-type reactions seen in some patients.

Investigators concluded that the material’s structure and high degree of sulfation allowed it to evade standard testing methods used at the time. Its presence at substantial concentrations also intensified suspicions of economically motivated adulteration, although establishing responsibility required separate investigative and enforcement work.

The FDA moved to introduce more sensitive screening techniques, including nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy and capillary electrophoresis, and manufacturers were directed to use enhanced methods to detect OSCS and related impurities.

## A global supply-chain warning

The heparin crisis is rapidly becoming more than a single-company recall. It exposes weaknesses in oversight of complex pharmaceutical supply chains, particularly for biologically derived ingredients that pass through several processors before reaching a finished-drug manufacturer.

It also demonstrates the limits of relying on specifications designed to confirm a drug’s expected characteristics without adequately searching for closely related adulterants. A contaminant engineered or selected to mimic heparin could satisfy older quality tests while posing risks those tests were never built to detect.

Federal officials say the investigation remains active. The immediate priorities are identifying all affected products, preventing further exposure, preserving the heparin supply and determining how the contaminant entered the manufacturing chain.

For hospitals and patients, the message is deliberately cautious: the reported reactions are serious, but heparin remains lifesaving and should not be withheld when medically necessary. The recall is intended to remove suspect products while regulators and manufacturers determine the full scope of one of the most consequential drug-safety investigations in recent years.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
**FDA Finds Unidentified Compound in Some Heparin Samples**

WASHINGTON — Federal health officials said some samples of the blood thinner heparin contained an unidentified glycan-like compound accounting for roughly 5% to 20% of the material, raising new questions about the drug’s production and supply chain.

The Food and Drug Administration said investigators had detected the substance while examining heparin linked to reports of severe allergic-type reactions and deaths. However, officials cautioned that they had not established whether the compound caused the adverse events.

Investigators also had not determined how the substance entered the heparin. The FDA said it remained unclear whether the compound was introduced accidentally during manufacturing or deliberately added at some point in production.

The agency was continuing chemical testing and tracing affected products through the supply chain. Officials emphasized that the finding represented a significant anomaly but did not, by itself, prove a connection to the reported deaths.
